desc: In this activity, students will explore the concept of air resistance by observing how a crumpled paper and a flat paper fall differently. They will then create a simple parachute using everyday materials and test how air resistance slows down falling objects. Through this hands-on activity, students will connect scientific concepts with real-life applications like parachutes.

units.desc: Students will understand the concept of air resistance, which is a force that opposes the motion of objects moving through air. They will learn that objects with a larger surface area experience more air resistance and fall more slowly, while objects with a smaller surface area fall faster. They will understand how air resistance is used in real life, such as in parachutes, which help in slow and safe landing.

Students will understand that a force is needed to start motion. Once the spinner starts moving, it continues due to inertia, which means objects in motion tend to stay in motion.
They will also learn that balance is important for smooth rotation, and friction can slow down movement. Reducing friction (using a central pivot like a toothpick) helps the spinner move more freely and for a longer time.

units.desc:
Students will be able to observe and explain how forces create motion.

Students will understand Newton’s Third Law of Motion, which states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. When air is pushed out of the balloon (action), the car moves forward (reaction).

They will also learn that force can create motion, and the direction of force affects how objects move.

units.desc:
Students will be able to observe and explain how applying force can change the shape and movement of an object.

They will understand that pressure and force help create a gripping action. When the cup is pressed, the flaps close inward, allowing the claw to grab objects. When released, the flaps open again.

Students will also learn that design and structure play an important role in how effectively a machine works.

units.desc:
Students will learn that many machines are inspired by nature—this concept is called biomimicry.

They will understand that when a force is applied by pulling a rope (tension), it creates movement in connected parts. In this model, pulling the threads causes the plastic “fingers” to close, allowing the arm to grip objects.

They will also explore how structures designed with multiple moving parts can work together like muscles in our body or claws in animals to perform tasks efficiently.

units.desc:
Students will learn that a balance weighing scale is a simple machine used to compare the weight of two objects.

They will understand the concept of equilibrium, where both sides of the scale are equal and balanced. When one side is heavier, it goes down, and the lighter side goes up—just like a see-saw.

They will also learn that balance depends on equal forces acting on both sides, helping us measure and compare weights accurately.
